title: Butter Chicken at Costco: How Indian Food Brands Are Storming America's Grocery Aisles
excerpt: From Quicklly's launch at 2,500 ALDI stores to Truly Indian's NEXTY Award nods, packaged Indian cuisine is muscling into mainstream American retail at an unprecedented pace.
body:
Walk into a Costco in the American Southeast and you might find something that would have been unthinkable a decade ago: a ready-to-heat butter chicken meal, made with grass-fed lamb and Himalayan basmati rice, sitting alongside the rotisserie chickens and frozen pizzas. Welcome to the new geography of Indian food in America — and it is being redrawn not in restaurant kitchens, but on grocery shelves.

## The Costco-ALDI Breakthrough

Quicklly, a Chicago-based Indian online marketplace, announced earlier this year that its "Just by Quicklly" line of ready-to-heat Indian meals has landed at two of America's most powerful retailers: Costco and ALDI. The Costco rollout covers 81 locations across the Southeast, with butter chicken as the flagship product. ALDI is carrying butter chicken and chicken tikka masala across 2,500 stores nationwide — one of the largest single launches of an Indian food product in American grocery history.

"Our vision is to help shape the next evolution of Indian cuisine through strategic partnerships that deliver elevated, immersive food experiences," said Quicklly founders Hanish Pahwa and Keval Raj. The meals are made with rBST-free dairy, antibiotic-free chicken, and come in packaging designed to stand out in the freezer aisle rather than blend into the "ethnic foods" section — a deliberate brand strategy.

Founded in 2017, Quicklly built its base as an online marketplace connecting Indian food suppliers with American consumers. The Costco and ALDI launch marks its leap from e-commerce niche to mainstream retail force.

## The NEXTY Effect

Quicklly is not alone. Truly Indian, a brand of ADF Foods — a fourth-generation family-owned company founded in 1932 — earned two finalist placements at the 2026 NEXTY Awards at Natural Products Expo West. The recognised products: a Tikka Masala Naan and a Crispy Chili Mango Chutney.

What makes the nods significant is the category positioning. Truly Indian's frozen naan is vegan, Non-GMO Project Verified, low-glycemic, Kosher, and Halal certified — checking nearly every box that drives purchasing decisions in the natural and specialty grocery channel. The company produces approximately 150,000 hand-stretched naans daily, each baked in traditional clay ovens at commercial scale. At $6.99 per pack, the price point hits the sweet spot between artisan credibility and mass-market accessibility.

Since launching in May 2024, Truly Indian has expanded to more than 1,300 stores nationwide, offering frozen and shelf-stable meals, samosas, naans, wraps, cooking sauces, and chutneys.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to industry data from Dataessential. The US ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion, and Indian food brands are expanding distribution across natural, conventional, and club channels simultaneously — a trifecta that few international cuisines have achieved at this pace.

The growth is happening despite headwinds. Tariff-related cost pressures and pricing volatility are affecting many global food categories, but retailers report sustained consumer demand for authentic Indian flavours. The appetite, it seems, is outrunning the economics.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, seeing butter chicken at Costco is more than a convenience — it is a marker of cultural arrival. For decades, Indian grocery shopping meant dedicated trips to specialty stores like Patel Brothers or online ordering from niche platforms. The migration of Indian staples into Costco and ALDI represents a normalisation that the community has long anticipated.

It also changes the dynamic at home. First-generation immigrants who grew up cooking dal and sabzi from scratch can now hand their American-born children a freezer meal that tastes close enough to home cooking to satisfy nostalgia, while being convenient enough to fit a life that does not revolve around a pressure cooker.

## The Bigger Play

The brands making this push are not positioning Indian food as exotic — they are positioning it as everyday. Quicklly's meals sit in the prepared-foods section, not the international aisle. Truly Indian's naan competes with other frozen bread products, not with a separate "Indian" sub-shelf. This shelf placement is strategic: it signals to mainstream American shoppers that Indian food belongs in their regular rotation, not their occasional adventure.

The grocery aisle, it turns out, may be where Indian cuisine finally completes its American mainstreaming — one butter chicken SKU at a time.
